m01: When a new king who didn't know Joseph ruled Egypt, my people's suffering began.
Under the blazing sun they mixed mud, shaped bricks and built Pithom and Rameses.
Even so, the midwives Shiphrah and Puah feared God and let the babies live.
m02: My mother hid me for three months, then laid me in a papyrus basket.
My sister stood a little way off, holding her breath, watching that basket among the reeds.
Pharaoh's daughter came to bathe and opened the basket — and I went back to my mother's arms to grow up.
m03: I grew up in the palace, but I struck down an Egyptian who was beating one of my people and hid him in the sand.
When word reached Pharaoh, I left everything and fled here to Midian.
I helped Reuel's daughters at the well, stayed in their home, and married Zipporah.
m04: I was leading my father-in-law Jethro's flock when I saw a bush that burned but didn't burn up.
From the middle of the flames He called my name. I took off my sandals and hid my face.
I kept backing away, so in the end the Lord gave me my brother Aaron to go with me.
m05: With Aaron I went into Pharaoh's palace and said, Let the people go to hold a festival.
Instead, Pharaoh stopped giving them straw for the bricks, yet demanded the same number of bricks.
The beaten foremen stood in our way, and with a broken heart I went back to the Lord.
m06: When I struck the Nile with my staff, the river turned to blood and the dead fish floated up.
Frogs and gnats, swarms of flies and hail, locusts and three days of darkness — the plagues kept coming.
Yet whenever a plague stopped, Pharaoh hardened his heart again. Now only the last plague is left.
m07: Every household killed a spotless lamb and, with hyssop, put its blood on the doorposts and the top of the door frame.
At midnight a great cry went up across all Egypt. There wasn't a house without a firstborn lost.
We wrapped our unrisen dough in our clothes, carried it on our shoulders and left Rameses that night.
m08: The long line that came out of Rameses reached Succoth here.
The coast road through Philistine land was shortest, but God led us by the wilderness road toward the Red Sea.
Look — by day the pillar of cloud, and by night the pillar of fire, never left the front of us.
m09: The sea was ahead and Pharaoh's chariots behind. The people cried out to me.
That night the pillar of cloud moved behind the camp — dark on Egypt's side, light on ours.
A strong east wind blew all night and laid the seabed bare, and we crossed on dry ground between walls of water.
m10: The morning after we crossed, pieces of broken chariots washed up on the calm shore.
On the wet sand, the Israelites and I lifted our voices in a song to the Lord.
Miriam took up her tambourine, and the women followed her, dancing. Listen to the sea breeze.
m11: We left the Red Sea and walked three days through the Desert of Shur without finding water.
When we finally found water at Marah, it was too bitter to drink, and the people grumbled against me.
The Lord showed me a piece of wood; I threw it into the water and the water became sweet. Afterward we reached Elim.
m12: In the second month after leaving Egypt, the food ran out and the whole community grumbled against us.
The day after the quail flew in, when the dew lifted, something like frost lay over the wilderness.
People looked at each other and asked, What is it? It tasted like wafers made with honey.
m13: There was no water at Rephidim either. The thirsty people crowded around me and quarreled.
With some of the elders, I walked ahead of the people holding the staff that had struck the Nile.
When water gushed from the rock, I called this place Massah and Meribah.
m14: Amalek came to attack, and Joshua went out to fight, while I went up the hill with Aaron and Hur.
Whenever I held up my hands, Israel won; whenever I lowered them, Amalek won.
When my arms grew heavy, Aaron and Hur sat me on a stone and held up my hands, one on each side.
m15: My father-in-law Jethro came to this wilderness, bringing my wife Zipporah and my two sons.
When I told him what the Lord had done to Pharaoh and Egypt, his face lit up.
The next day he saw me judging cases alone all day long, and he shared his wisdom with me.
m16: In the third month after leaving Egypt, we camped in front of this red peak.
The people washed their clothes, made themselves clean and waited for the third day.
That morning, amid thunder and trumpet blasts, the mountain smoked and shook. Look up at that mountain.
m17: Smoke wrapped the whole mountain, and fire blazed at its top.
From within it God Himself spoke the Ten Words, and the people listened, holding their breath.
Trembling, the people stayed far back, and I went alone into the thick darkness.
m18: Early in the morning I built an altar at the foot of the mountain and set up twelve stone pillars for the twelve tribes.
Then I read the Book of the Covenant, the Lord's words I had written down, for the people to hear.
With seventy elders I went up the mountain, and under a sky as clear as sapphire we ate and drank.
m19: When I stayed long on the mountain, the people crowded around Aaron and told him to make them a god.
I came down with the stone tablets in my arms and saw a crowd dancing around a golden calf.
I threw down the tablets and broke them, then burned the calf and ground it to powder.
m20: After the golden calf, I pleaded with Him to remember that this people was His people.
The Lord said He would put me in a cleft of the rock and cover me with His hand.
At dawn the next day, I climbed this mountain alone with two newly cut stone tablets. Look at that rock.
m21: In the middle of the camp, gold-covered frames rose up one by one on silver bases.
I put the tablets of the covenant in the ark and set the table, the lampstand and the gold altar of incense in their places.
Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting and the glory filled it, so that even I could not go in.
m22: After we left Sinai, the people longed for meat and wept at the doors of their tents.
A wind from the sea drove in flocks of quail, piled two cubits deep around the camp.
While the meat was still between their teeth, a plague struck. That's why it's called Kibroth Hattaavah, the graves of craving.
m23: I chose twelve men, one leader from each tribe, and sent them to explore that land.
They came back from the Valley of Eshcol carrying a cluster of grapes on a pole between two of them.
Joshua and Caleb cried out, Don't be afraid! But the whole community wanted to stone them.
m24: Korah, Dathan and Abiram led two hundred fifty men to stand against us.
The ground under them split open and swallowed them, and fire consumed the men holding censers.
And look — overnight Aaron's staff sprouted, blossomed and bore ripe almonds.
m25: My sister Miriam died here, and in our grief even the water ran out.
When the people crowded around and quarreled, Aaron and I fell face down at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
I struck the rock twice with my staff. People called that water Meribah.
m26: We left Kadesh and came to this red rocky mountain on the border of Edom.
With my brother Aaron and his son Eleazar, I climbed the mountain while the whole community watched.
Only Eleazar and I came back down. All Israel mourned for thirty days.
m27: To go around the land of Edom, we turned back toward the Red Sea road.
The road grew long, the people spoke against God and me, and venomous snakes came into the camp.
The people came pleading to me, and I prayed to the Lord for them.
m28: Sihon king of the Amorites wouldn't let us pass; he gathered all his people and came out to Jahaz to stop us.
Israel took the land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and settled in Sihon's city, Heshbon.
We also won the battle against Og king of Bashan, and the plains east of the Jordan became our first land.
m29: Balak king of Moab looked down on our camp and trembled, so he sent for Balaam to curse us.
On the way an angel with a sword blocked the road, but only Balaam's donkey saw it.
Yet every time Balaam opened his mouth, blessings poured out instead of curses.
m30: As the forty years in the wilderness drew to an end, the new generation raised there sat down before me.
Pointing to the palm groves of Jericho across the river, I spoke with all the strength I had left.
We were Pharaoh's slaves, but the Lord brought us out with a mighty hand.
m31: I left the people on the plains of Moab and climbed alone to this top of Pisgah.
I was a hundred and twenty, but my eyes were not dim. The Lord showed me the whole land.
From Gilead in the north to Dan, to the sea in the west and the Negev in the south — look at that land with me.
m32: The days of mourning ended, and the tents were quiet in the shade of the acacias at Shittim.
Then the Lord told Joshua son of Nun to cross the Jordan with the people.
Joshua told the officers: In three days we cross — get your food ready.
m33: Two spies, sent secretly from Shittim, slipped into Rahab's house, built into this city wall.
Rahab hid them under stalks of flax on her roof and sent the king's men off toward the Jordan fords.
Then she let them down from her window by a rope, outside the city. Can you see the window in that wall?
m34: It was the spring harvest, and the Jordan was overflowing its banks.
As soon as the feet of the priests carrying the ark touched the water, the water upstream stopped like a dam.
All the people crossed on the dry riverbed, and the manna that had fallen for forty years soon stopped.
m35: Jericho had its gates shut tight, and the Lord told us not to use swords, but to walk.
For six days we circled the city without a word — only the sound of trumpets and footsteps.
The city fell, but everyone in Rahab's house, where the scarlet cord hung, came out alive.
m36: About three thousand men went up, but they were chased from the gate, and thirty-six fell on this slope.
I tore my clothes, and with the elders, dust on our heads, I lay face down before the ark until evening.
As the lots narrowed down, Achan was found out — and only after that did we take this city by ambush.
m37: Mount Ebal to the north and Mount Gerizim to the south face each other across this valley.
As Moses had commanded, I built an altar on Mount Ebal and copied the law onto its stones.
Half the people stood in front of one mountain and half in front of the other. Take a look around this valley.
m38: When the armies of five kings surrounded Gibeon, the Gibeonites rushed messengers to Gilgal.
I marched up the mountain roads all night, fell on the enemy at dawn, and great hailstones poured down on the slope of Beth Horon.
That day the sun stood still in the middle of the sky and did not go down for about a whole day.
m39: After the days of fighting across the Jordan, the whole community set up the tent of meeting here at Shiloh.
But seven tribes still hadn't received their share, and they just kept hesitating.
Those who surveyed the land came back, and at last the promise became land with names on it.
m40: Many years later, I gathered all the tribes of Israel here at Shechem once again.
I told them the long story, from Terah's household beyond the River to the day we crossed the Jordan.
On the day we made the covenant, I set up a large stone as a witness under the oak by the sanctuary.
